principal_characters: Mr Weston; Michael; Luke Bird; Mr Grunter; Tamar; the villagers

Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem; The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
description: The founding text of modern Black American literature: the colour line and the double consciousness. It is a prose work of 1903 by W. E. B. Du Bois; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Du Bois combines history, sociology, memoir, fiction and the spiritual into fourteen essays that analyse the position of the Black American after emancipation: the Freedmen's Bureau, Booker T. Washington, the Black church, the sorrow songs and the death of his own son.
narrative_structure: Fourteen essays, with a preface and the spirituals as epigraphs. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
principal_characters: Du Bois as author; Booker T. Washington; Alexander Crummell; the Black folk
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the essay and the sociological survey side by side.
historical_context: The United States after Reconstruction, and the conditions of Black American life in 1903. The record dates the work as composed between 1902 and 1903 and first published in 1903 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; critical essay and the modern review.

McClurg and Company of Chicago in April 1903, nine of the fourteen chapters having appeared in The Atlantic Monthly, The World's Work, The New World and elsewhere between 1897 and 1903; the 'Sorrow Songs' carry the slave-song notations of the Fisk Jubilee tradition. title: Darkwater: Voices from Within the Veil

plot_or_argument: Du Bois gathers essays, short stories, poems and allegories on the colour line across the world: the African, the American city, the Black woman, the First World War and the future of the darker races, in a book that is both a manifesto and a work of literature.
narrative_structure: Nine essays and sketches, with poems and allegories. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
principal_characters: Du Bois as author; the darker races; the Black woman; the returned soldier
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. title: The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man
description: The founding novel of the Black American passing narrative: a man who crosses the colour line. It is a prose fiction work of 1912 by James Weldon Johnson; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: An unnamed narrator, born in the South to a Black mother and a white father, grows up as a talented musician, travels in Europe, witnesses a lynching in the South, and finally decides to pass as white and live in the North, ending with his regret for the heritage he has abandoned.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative in eleven chapters, from the South to Europe and the North. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
principal_characters: the unnamed narrator; his mother; his father; the millionaire; the woman in Paris
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person passing narrative.

The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1912 and first published in 1912 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
literary_significance: The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man was the founding novel of the Black American passing narrative and the first novel by a Black American to be published anonymously as a genuine autobiography: its portrait of the colour line made it a central text of American literature and a direct ancestor of Invisible Man.

title: God's Trombones: Seven Negro Sermons in Verse
description: The great poem of the Black folk sermon: the creation, the flood and the judgement. It is a verse work of 1927 by James Weldon Johnson; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem; Religious Lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Seven sermons in free verse — 'The Creation', 'The Prodigal Son', 'Go Down, Death', 'Noah Built the Ark', 'The Judgment Day' — in which the Black preacher's voice is rendered with its cadence, its imagery and its authority.
narrative_structure: Seven sermons in free verse. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience. A collection of devotional lyrics, each in the hymn stanza or the short rhymed form, written for meditation or for congregational use.
principal_characters: the preacher; God; Adam; Noah; the Prodigal Son
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person passing narrative.
historical_context: The rural Black South of the nineteenth century, and the Black church tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem; religious lyric.
literary_significance: God's Trombones created the sermon in verse and gave the Black folk preacher his permanent literary form: 'The Creation' and 'Go Down, Death' are among the great American poems of the century, and the collection founded the modern literature of the Black sermon.

title: Quicksand
description: Larsen's first novel: a mixed-race woman's search for a place and a self. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Nella Larsen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Helga Crane, the daughter of a Danish mother and a Black father, leaves her teaching post in the South, moves to Harlem, to Denmark and back again, searching for a home and a self, and ends in a disastrous marriage and childbirth in the rural South.
narrative_structure: A novel in twenty-five chapters, from the South to Harlem to Denmark and back. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
principal_characters: Helga Crane; Naxos; Anne Grey; the Dr Andersons; Herr Dahl; Rev. Pleasant Green
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the short novel of the interior life.
historical_context: The United States, Harlem and Denmark in the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro; The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
